The sign of \(W = Fd\cos\theta\) is fixed by the angle \(\theta\) between the force and the displacement: positive if \(\theta < 90^{\circ}\), negative if \(\theta > 90^{\circ}\).

(a) The man pulls the rope upward and the bucket moves upward, so \(\theta = 0^{\circ}\): the work is **positive**.

(b) Gravity acts downward while the bucket moves upward, so \(\theta = 180^{\circ}\): the work is **negative**.

(c) Friction on a body sliding down an incline acts up the incline, opposite to the displacement, so \(\theta = 180^{\circ}\): the work is **negative**.

(d) Uniform velocity means zero net force, so the applied force just balances friction and acts along the motion, \(\theta = 0^{\circ}\): the work is **positive**.

(e) The resistive force of air always opposes the bob's velocity, \(\theta = 180^{\circ}\): the work is **negative** (which is why the pendulum comes to rest).

Answer: (a) positive, (b) negative, (c) negative, (d) positive, (e) negative.

Take \(g = 9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).

Frictional force \(f = \mu m g = 0.1\times 2\times 9.8 = 1.96\,\text{N}\)

Net force \(= 7 - 1.96 = 5.04\,\text{N}\), so the acceleration is

\(a = \dfrac{5.04}{2} = 2.52\,\text{m s}^{-2}\)

Starting from rest, in \(t = 10\,\text{s}\) the body travels

\(s = \dfrac{1}{2}at^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\times 2.52\times 100 = 126\,\text{m}\), and reaches \(v = at = 25.2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

(a) Work done by the applied force \(= 7\times 126 = 882\,\text{J}\)

(b) Work done by friction \(= -1.96\times 126 = -247\,\text{J}\) (negative, since friction opposes the motion)

(c) Work done by the net force \(= 5.04\times 126 = 635\,\text{J}\)

(d) Change in kinetic energy \(= \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - 0 = \dfrac{1}{2}\times 2\times (25.2)^2 = 635\,\text{J}\)

Interpretation: (c) and (d) are equal, which is exactly the work-energy theorem — the change in kinetic energy equals the work done by the NET force, not by the applied force alone. The applied force supplies \(882\,\text{J}\), of which \(247\,\text{J}\) is removed by friction and appears as heat.

Answer: (a) \(882\,\text{J}\); (b) \(-247\,\text{J}\); (c) \(635\,\text{J}\); (d) \(635\,\text{J}\).

The particle can only be where its kinetic energy \(K = E - V(x)\) is non-negative, i.e. where \(V(x) \le E\). A region with \(V(x) > E\) is forbidden. The minimum total energy the particle can have is the minimum value of \(V(x)\).

(a) \(V = 0\) for \(x < a\) and \(V = V_0\) for \(x > a\), with \(0 < E < V_0\). Since \(E < V_0\), the region \(x > a\) is forbidden. Minimum total energy \(= 0\).
Context: a particle running into a step barrier — for example a ball rolling towards a raised step it has too little energy to climb.

(b) The potential rises in steps and every plateau lies above the marked \(E\), including the lowest one at \(x < 0\). So \(V(x) > E\) everywhere shown and the particle cannot be found in ANY of the regions. The minimum total energy it must have is the lowest plateau value, that of \(V(x)\) for \(x < 0\).
Context: a particle facing a staircase of successive barriers, as in a series of potential steps.

(c) \(V = V_0\) for \(x < a\) and \(x > b\), and \(V = -V_1\) for \(a < x < b\), with \(0 < E < V_0\). The regions \(x < a\) and \(x > b\) are forbidden; the particle is trapped in the well \(a < x < b\). Minimum total energy \(= -V_1\).
Context: a square potential well — a bound particle such as a nucleon inside a nucleus, or an electron confined in a metal.

(d) \(V = -V_1\) for \(|x| < a/2\); the potential rises steeply to a peak at \(|x| = a/2\) and then falls away, crossing the level \(E\) at \(|x| = b/2\). The forbidden regions are therefore \(-b/2 < x < -a/2\) and \(a/2 < x < b/2\), where \(V(x) > E\). Minimum total energy \(= -V_1\).
Context: a well flanked by barriers — the potential energy of an alpha particle inside a nucleus facing the Coulomb barrier, or of the atoms in a diatomic molecule.

The particle's total energy is \(E = K + V\), and its kinetic energy cannot be negative:

\(K = E - V(x) = 1 - \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2 \ge 0\)

With \(k = 0.5\,\text{N m}^{-1}\),

\(1 - \dfrac{1}{2}(0.5)x^2 \ge 0 \;\Rightarrow\; 1 - 0.25\,x^2 \ge 0 \;\Rightarrow\; x^2 \le 4\)

so \(|x| \le 2\,\text{m}\).

At \(x = \pm 2\,\text{m}\) the equality holds, so \(K = 0\): the particle is momentarily at rest. Beyond these points \(V(x)\) would exceed \(1\,\text{J}\) and the kinetic energy would be negative, which is impossible. Hence the particle must turn back at \(x = \pm 2\,\text{m}\).

Answer: the turning points are \(x = \pm 2\,\text{m}\).

(a) At the expense of the ROCKET's energy. The casing and the air rub against each other, and the heat generated is drawn from the rocket's own kinetic (mechanical) energy, so the rocket slows down. The atmosphere is not the source — it is essentially at rest and has no energy to give up.

(b) Because the gravitational force is CONSERVATIVE, and the work done by a conservative force over any closed path is zero. Over one complete orbit the comet returns to its starting point, so \(W = V(x_i) - V(x_f) = 0\). The force need not be perpendicular to the velocity at each instant: the positive work done as the comet approaches the sun is exactly cancelled by the negative work done as it recedes.

(c) For a satellite in a (near) circular orbit of radius \(r\), the kinetic energy is \(K = GMm/2r\) and the total energy is \(E = -GMm/2r\), so \(K = -E\). Drag makes the total energy \(E\) more negative, which means \(r\) decreases — and since \(K = GMm/2r\), a smaller \(r\) gives a LARGER kinetic energy. The potential energy falls by twice as much as the total energy lost, and the difference goes into kinetic energy, so the satellite speeds up even while losing energy overall.

(d) In case (i) the man supports the \(15\,\text{kg}\) mass with a vertical (upward) force while his displacement is horizontal, so the angle between force and displacement is \(90^{\circ}\) and the work done on the mass is ZERO.
In case (ii) he pulls the rope horizontally through \(2\,\text{m}\), which raises the hanging \(15\,\text{kg}\) mass by \(2\,\text{m}\) against gravity:
\(W = mgh = 15\times 9.8\times 2 = 294\,\text{J}\)

Answer: the work done is greater in case (ii), namely \(294\,\text{J}\) against zero in case (i).

The body moves only along the \(z\)-axis, so its displacement is

\(\mathbf{d} = 4\hat{\mathbf{k}}\,\text{m}\)

Work done by a constant force is the scalar product

\(W = \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{d} = (-\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 2\hat{\mathbf{j}} + 3\hat{\mathbf{k}})\cdot(4\hat{\mathbf{k}})\)

Only the \(z\)-components contribute, since \(\hat{\mathbf{i}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{k}} = \hat{\mathbf{j}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{k}} = 0\):

\(W = 3\times 4 = 12\,\text{J}\)

The \(x\)- and \(y\)-components of the force do no work because there is no displacement along those directions.

Answer: \(W = 12\,\text{J}\).

Both particles are non-relativistic here, so \(K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2\), giving \(v = \sqrt{2K/m}\).

For the electron, \(K_e = 10\,\text{keV} = 10\times 10^{3}\times 1.60\times 10^{-19} = 1.6\times 10^{-15}\,\text{J}\)

\(v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2\times 1.6\times 10^{-15}}{9.11\times 10^{-31}}} = 5.93\times 10^{7}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

For the proton, \(K_p = 100\,\text{keV} = 1.6\times 10^{-14}\,\text{J}\)

\(v_p = \sqrt{\dfrac{2\times 1.6\times 10^{-14}}{1.67\times 10^{-27}}} = 4.38\times 10^{6}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

So the ELECTRON is faster, even though it has ten times LESS kinetic energy, because its mass is about \(1800\) times smaller.

\(\dfrac{v_e}{v_p} = \dfrac{5.93\times 10^{7}}{4.38\times 10^{6}} \approx 13.5\)

Answer: the electron is faster; \(v_e : v_p \approx 13.5 : 1\).

Take \(g = 9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) and the density of water as \(10^{3}\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\).

Mass of the drop:

\(m = \rho\times\dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = 10^{3}\times\dfrac{4}{3}\pi(2\times 10^{-3})^3 = 3.35\times 10^{-5}\,\text{kg}\)

The work done by gravity depends only on the vertical drop, not on the speed, so each half of the journey (\(250\,\text{m}\)) gives the same amount:

\(W_1 = W_2 = mgh = 3.35\times 10^{-5}\times 9.8\times 250 = 0.082\,\text{J}\)

Total work done by gravity over the whole \(500\,\text{m}\):

\(W_g = 0.164\,\text{J}\)

The drop starts from rest and reaches the ground at \(10\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), so

\(\Delta K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - 0 = \dfrac{1}{2}\times 3.35\times 10^{-5}\times 100 = 1.68\times 10^{-3}\,\text{J}\)

By the work-energy theorem, \(\Delta K = W_g + W_r\), so

\(W_r = \Delta K - W_g = 1.68\times 10^{-3} - 0.164 = -0.163\,\text{J}\)

The resistive work is negative, as it must be, and it removes almost all of the energy gravity supplies.

Answer: work done by gravity is \(0.082\,\text{J}\) in each half (\(0.164\,\text{J}\) in total); work done by the resistive force over the whole journey is \(-0.163\,\text{J}\).
